nameStory: The Thin-spined Jumping Spider gets its name from the delicate, slender spines that run along its legs - much finer than those of its thick-spined cousin. Like all jumping spiders, it earned the 'jumping' part of its name from its incredible ability to leap many times its own body length to catch prey or escape danger.
description: The Thin-spined Jumping Spider is a small, compact hunter with the characteristic stocky build and large forward-facing eyes that make jumping spiders so distinctive. These tiny acrobats typically measure less than half an inch in body length, with females slightly larger than males. Their bodies are covered in fine hairs that give them a somewhat fuzzy appearance, and they move with the quick, jerky motions typical of their family. Unlike web-building spiders, these active hunters stalk their prey during the day.

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Four large eyes face forward like headlights, with the two center eyes noticeably larger and more prominent - they feel almost like they're looking right back at you

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, rectangular body that feels solid and chunky, like a tiny fuzzy box with legs - quite different from the elongated abdomen of web spiders

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves in quick, stop-and-go jerky motions, often turning to face you directly and raising its front legs in a boxer-like stance when approached

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small spider, with body length typically under half an inch - about the size of a large ant or small ladybug

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Often displays subtle patterns or bands across the abdomen, though coloration can be quite variable from brown to gray tones

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates no hunting web - only spins small silk retreats or safety lines, so you'll find them actively moving on surfaces rather than waiting in webs

habitat: Look for Thin-spined Jumping Spiders on tree bark, fence posts, stone walls, and the sides of buildings where they hunt for small insects. They prefer sunny, exposed surfaces where they can bask in warmth while scanning for prey. In New England, they're often found in mixed forests, suburban gardens, and anywhere there are vertical surfaces with good hunting opportunities.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter retreats and become active on warm, sunny days. Look for them sunning themselves on tree bark and fence posts.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most visible hunting during daylight hours. Mating displays and courtship behaviors are most common in early to mid-summer.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active into early fall, with females creating egg sacs before seeking winter shelter. Activity decreases as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter in silk-lined retreats under bark, in rock crevices, or other protected spots, remaining inactive until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Jumping spiders have better color vision than most mammals and can see into the ultraviolet spectrum - they're actually watching you with vision that's far superior to your own, which explains why they seem to track your movements so intently!
confusionNotes: The Thin-spined Jumping Spider is easily confused with other small jumping spiders, but the key is in the name - look closely at the leg spines with a magnifying glass to see the fine, delicate spines rather than thick, robust ones. Remember: thin spines, thin name.
contextualKnowledge: The genus name Tutelina comes from Latin meaning 'little guardian' or 'protector,' possibly referring to how these spiders seem to watch over their territory with their alert, vigilant behavior and prominent eyes.
compareHints: Among its Tutelina relatives in New England, the Thin-spined Jumping Spider is distinguished by its delicate leg spines compared to the robust spines of the Thick-spined Jumping Spider. Hart's Jumping Spider tends to be found in different microhabitats and may show different coloration patterns. The leg spine thickness really is the most reliable way to separate these closely related species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Hart's Jumping Spider differs from its close relatives like the Thin-spined Jumping Spider by having a more robust, stocky build rather than an elongated appearance.
The Thick-spined Jumping Spider differs from Hart's Jumping Spider and the Thin-spined Jumping Spider primarily in the robustness of its leg spines - they're noticeably thicker and more substantial.
Distinguishing between Tutelina species requires very close examination and is challenging even for experts.
